A glint inside of Abrahm Lincoln's Cabinet
appointment‸before—one item of many.—
body.p: ‸give head ital. When While it was h hanging in suspense who should be appointed Secretary of the Interior, (to take the place of Caleb ? Smith) the nom choice was very close between Jim Harlan & Col. Jesse K. Dubois of Illinois. The latter had many friends. He was competent, he was honest & he was a man. Mr. Harlan, was pressed in the race, finally gain'd the Methodist interest, & got himself to be considered as identified with it, & his appointment was apparently asked for by that powerful body. Bishop Simpson of Philadelphia came on & spoke for ‸the appointment.. The President was much perplexed. Col. Col. Dubois's The reasons for appointing Col. Dubois were very strong, almost insuperable,— yet the argument for Mr. Harlan, under the circumstancesadroit position he had placed himself, in, was heavy. Those who pressed him adduced the magnitude of the Methodists as a body, their loyalty more ‸general & genuine than any other sect,

that thy represented the West, & had a right to be heard—That al all ‸or all the 2 other great denominations had their representatives in the Heads of the government, that thy as a body ‸& the great secretarian power of the West, formally asked Mr. Harlan's appointment— that he h hadwas for of them, having been a Methodist minister, that it would not do to offend them, but was necessarybesthighly necessary to propitiate them.

Mr. Lincoln thought deeply over the whole matter. He was for a while in more than usual tribulation on the subject ‸Let it be enough to say that though Mr. Harlan finally received the ap Secretaryship, Col. Dubois came as near being appointed Secretary of the Interior as a man could, & not he. But the President The discussion was ‸finally made one night about 10 o'clock. Bishop Simpson & other clergymen & p leading persons in Mr. Harlan's behalf, had been talking long & vehemently with the President. A member of Congress who was pressing Col. Dubois's claims, was in waiting. The President said had told the Bishop that he would make a decision that evening & that he would thought it unnecessary
